subtopics.title: Key Facts & Syntax Cheat-Sheet
subtopics.subtitle: Sizes, precedence, defaults and rules from every section, each with the code that shows it

concepts.text: Programming MCQs turn on a few dozen facts: sizes and ranges, precedence, what a construct defaults to, and the exact rule a keyword enforces. This page lists them section by section with the smallest code that shows each rule. Cover a block, write the fact from memory, then check the subtopic for the reasoning.
1. C basics: tokens, types, operators, I/O, control flow, functions, arrays

items: C89 has 32 keywords; identifiers start with a letter or underscore, contain letters, digits, underscores, and are case-sensitive.
Constants: integer (10, 012 octal, 0xA hex, 10U, 10L), floating (3.14, 2e3, 3.0f), character ('A', '\n', '\0'), string ("text", stored with a terminating '\0').
main returns int; a program starts at main and ends when main returns or exit() is called.

concepts.text:
int a = 5;
printf("%d %d", a++, ++a);   /* order of evaluation is unspecified: never write this */
int b = 7 / 2;                  /* 3: integer division truncates toward zero */
int c = -7 % 3;                 /* -1: sign of % follows the dividend */
int d = (1, 2, 3);              /* 3: comma yields the last operand */
Control-flow rules that decide output questions:
items: switch works on an integral type (int, char, enum); without break, execution falls through into the following cases.
do-while runs its body at least once; while and for test first. for(;;) is an infinite loop.
break leaves the innermost loop or switch; continue jumps to the next iteration (in a for loop the increment still runs).
if (x = 5) assigns and is always true; = versus == is the classic trap.
A semicolon after for(...) or while(...) makes an empty loop body.
Arguments are passed by value; to change the caller's variable pass its address and dereference (swap via pointers).
A prototype declares name, return type and parameter types before use; a definition supplies the body.
Every recursive function needs a base case; each call adds a stack frame, so deep recursion can overflow the stack.
static local variables keep their value between calls; automatic locals are re-created each call.

concepts.plainText: factorial(n) = n × factorial(n−1) with factorial(0) = 1; n + 1 calls in total

items: int a[10] holds a[0] … a[9]; total size = n × sizeof(type); a 2-D array is stored row-major, address of a[i][j] = base + (i × cols + j) × sizeof(type).
An array name decays to a pointer to its first element: a ≡ &a[0], a[i] ≡ *(a + i); sizeof(a) is the whole array only in the declaring scope.
A C-string ends with '\0': strlen("EXAM") = 4 but sizeof("EXAM") = 5. strcmp returns 0 for equal strings; strcpy/strcat need enough room in the destination.
scanf("%s") stops at the first space; use fgets to read a line.

concepts.plainText: p + i moves i elements, not i bytes; pointer difference is measured in elements

concepts.text:
int a[] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
int *p = a;               /* p -> a[0] */
printf("%d", *(p + 2));  /* 30 */
printf("%d", *p++);      /* 10, then p -> a[1]: postfix ++ binds tighter than * */
int *q = malloc(5 * sizeof *q);  /* check q != NULL; free(q) when done */

items: int *p declares a pointer; &x gives an address; *p reads or writes the pointee. NULL pointers must not be dereferenced.
const int *p: data read-only through p;  int *const p: the pointer itself is fixed.
malloc returns uninitialised memory, calloc zeroed memory; realloc resizes; every malloc needs one free. Using freed memory = dangling pointer.
Passing a pointer lets a function modify the caller's variable; passing an array always passes a pointer.

rows: one at a time, same address
read (must exist) / write (truncate or create) / append (create if missing)
read and write; w+ truncates, a+ appends
random access; ftell gives the position; rewind goes to the start

items: class members are private by default, struct members public; protected is visible to derived classes.
A constructor has the class name, no return type, and runs when an object is created; a destructor is ~Name(), takes no arguments and runs when the object dies (reverse order of construction).
Copy constructor: Name(const Name &other) — the parameter must be a reference; Box b = a; and passing/returning by value invoke it.
new/delete for single objects, new[]/delete[] for arrays; mixing them is undefined behaviour.

static data member: one copy per class, defined outside the class; static member function has no this. const member function cannot modify members; only const functions can be called on const objects.
friend functions/classes access private members but are not members, are not inherited and friendship is not transitive.
Default arguments are supplied from the rightmost parameter; inline is a request; references must be initialised and cannot be reseated.
Constructors run base first, then derived; destructors run derived first, then base. Base constructors get arguments through the initialiser list.
Multipath (diamond) inheritance duplicates the common base; declare it a virtual base class to keep one copy.
Operators that cannot be overloaded: ::  .  .*  ?:  sizeof. Overloading cannot change precedence, associativity or the number of operands.
operator++() is prefix, operator++(int) is postfix. Binary operators as members take one argument; as friends they take two.
Basic → class conversion uses a constructor; class → basic uses a conversion operator (operator double()); class → class uses either, in the destination constructor or the source conversion function.
A base-class pointer to a derived object calls the base version unless the function is virtual; virtual gives dynamic (late) binding through the vtable.
virtual void f() = 0; is a pure virtual function; a class with one is abstract and cannot be instantiated, though pointers and references to it are allowed.
Make the destructor virtual when deleting derived objects through base pointers. Constructors cannot be virtual; static and friend functions cannot be virtual.

rows: minimum field width for the next output only
significant digits, or decimals with fixed

items: ifstream reads, ofstream writes, fstream both; modes ios::in, ios::out, ios::app (append), ios::ate (start at end), ios::trunc, ios::binary, combined with |.
Check is_open()/fail(); eof() becomes true only after a read fails past the end.
seekg/tellg move and report the get pointer, seekp/tellp the put pointer, relative to ios::beg, ios::cur or ios::end.
A function template is instantiated per type at compile time; an exact non-template overload is preferred over a template.

STL = containers (vector, list, deque, set, map, stack, queue, priority_queue) + algorithms (sort, find, count, reverse, accumulate) + iterators (input, output, forward, bidirectional, random access).
vector gives O(1) random access and amortised O(1) push_back; list gives O(1) insert/erase anywhere but no random access; map keys are ordered and unique, multimap allows duplicates.
catch blocks are tried in order, so catch derived exceptions before base ones; catch (...) must be last; throw; rethrows the current exception.
noexcept (C++11) replaces the old throw() specification; an uncaught exception calls std::terminate.
Catch by reference to avoid slicing and copying; throw by value.

rows: Class default access / struct default access

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Chapter 3 Syntax & Output Drill

Most output and compile-error questions yield to the same four checks, applied in order. First fix the type of every operand: int or double, char promoted to int, array or pointer, base or derived. Next group the expression by precedence and associativity, then apply side effects one statement at a time, noting where a value is copied and where a pointer or reference reaches the original. Finally ask what is printed and in which format, and for C++ which constructor, destructor or override actually runs.

Output: 5 8 7| 10|11 |2.50|Ca

x = *p++ + 1   postfix ++ binds first: *(p++) reads a[0] = 4, x = 5, p -> a[1]
*p             now a[1] = 8
y              7 / 2 = 3 (integer), 3 * 2 = 6, 7 % 2 = 1, so y = 7
first, next()  static n survives calls: 10, then 11 (taken in separate
               statements, because printf's arguments have no fixed order)
%3d / %-3d     " 10" right-justified and "11 " left-justified in width 3
%.2f           5 / 2.0 is the double 2.5, printed as 2.50
%c             'A' + 2 = 67 = 'C', and 97 = 'a' (ASCII)

rows: *(p++) reads the value and moves the pointer; (*p)++ changes the value
(a > b) > c, where a > b is 0 or 1
c holds 1 or 0, not the character
Undefined behaviour; fix the specifier or cast
The operand is not evaluated (except for a VLA)

concepts.text:
Output: B M D D.who B.who ~D ~M ~B

new D        base part first (B), then the members in declaration
             order (M), then the body of D()
p->who()     who is virtual, so the object's real class decides: D.who
p->B::who()  a qualified name switches dispatch off: B.who
delete p     ~B is virtual, so ~D runs first, then the member (~M),
             then the base (~B); without a virtual ~B this delete
             would be undefined behaviour

rows: Private base members are never accessible; the rest take the stricter of their own access and the inheritance mode
class D : B (private by default) hides all of B from D's users
The static type decides which names exist; virtual only changes which body runs
A Base* cannot call a member declared only in Derived
Base object initialised from a derived one
Only the base part is copied (slicing)
Virtual calls on the copy run the base version
T is deduced from the arguments without conversions; an equally good non-template wins
big(2, 2.5) fails for template <class T> T big(T, T)
vector: fast index and push_back; list: fast insert anywhere; set/map: sorted unique keys
m[k] inserts a missing key; m.at(k) throws out_of_range
Handlers are tried in order and match the exact type, a base class or a pointer conversion
throw 'x' skips catch (int); catch derived before base
catch (...) must be the last handler; throw; rethrows the current object

concepts.text: Compile errors that revision questions like to hide:
items: Assigning to an array name (a = b; or a++): an array is not a modifiable lvalue.
Two case labels with the same constant value, or a case label that is not an integer constant.
Calling a non-const member function on a const object, or passing a const object to a non-const reference parameter.
Creating an object of an abstract class, or calling through a base pointer a member that only the derived class declares.
Using a private or protected member from main, including one made private by private inheritance.
In C, assigning to the result of ?: (C++ allows it when both branches are lvalues of the same type).

concepts.text: When the options differ in one character or one step, the question tests a single rule. Find where a value is copied instead of referenced, where integer division truncates, where a promotion or conversion happens, or where a static or virtual rule applies, and re-check just that step. Write the partial results beside each line instead of keeping them in your head.

formulas.plainText: Signed and unsigned n-bit integer ranges
Array size and row-major address of a[i][j]
Pointer arithmetic scales by the pointee size
Union size is the largest member; struct size is the sum plus padding
strlen excludes the terminator; sizeof of a literal includes it

notes.text: Output-prediction questions almost always hinge on one of: integer division, % with a negative operand, a++ versus ++a, missing break in switch, a stray semicolon after a loop header, or an array name used as a pointer. Check those five before computing anything.

Defaults that flip between C and C++: class members are private but struct members are public; C passes everything by value while C++ adds references; new/delete pair with each other and never with malloc/free; catch (...) must come last.
Sizes are platform-dependent, so a well-set question states them; if it does not, assume char 1, int 4, float 4, double 8, and remember sizeof("text") counts the terminating null.

formulas.title: Integer ranges
formulas.description: n is the number of bits: 8 for char, 16 for short, 32 for int on typical compilers.

formulas.title: Array size and 2-D address
formulas.plainText: size = n × sizeof(type);  &a[i][j] = base + (i × cols + j) × sizeof(type)
formulas.description: Row-major storage: all of row 0, then row 1, and so on.

formulas.title: Pointer arithmetic
formulas.plainText: p + i = address of p + i × sizeof(*p)
formulas.description: Adding i moves i elements; subtracting two pointers gives an element count.

formulas.title: struct and union sizes
formulas.plainText: union: largest member;  struct: sum of members plus any padding
formulas.description: Padding aligns members, so a struct can be larger than the plain sum.

flashcards.front: Which five C++ operators cannot be overloaded?
What do strlen("HELLO") and sizeof("HELLO") return, and why do they differ?
flashcards.back: 5 and 6: sizeof counts the terminating '\0' that strlen stops at.

flashcards.front: State the constructor and destructor order for class D derived from class B.
flashcards.back: Construction: B then D. Destruction: D then B (reverse). Base constructor arguments are passed through D's initialiser list.

questions.explanation: y = x++ stores the old value 10 and then makes x 11; z = ++x first makes x 12 and stores 12. Each increment is in its own statement, so the result is well defined: x = 12, y = 10, z = 12. (Writing x++ + ++x in one expression would instead be undefined behaviour.)

questions.questionText: Assuming sizeof(int) is 4, what does sizeof(arr) return for int arr[3][4]; inside the scope where it is declared?
questions.explanation: 3 × 4 = 12 elements × 4 bytes = 48 bytes; sizeof gives the whole array, not the element count.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a C++ class is correct?
options: Its members are public unless declared otherwise
A static member function can use the this pointer
A const member function may not modify the object's data members
A friend function is a member of the class
questions.explanation: const member functions promise not to change the object. Class members default to private, static functions have no this, and friends are non-members.

questions.questionText: Given int a[5] = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}; int *p = a + 1; what does printf("%d", *(p + 2)); print?
questions.explanation: p points at a[1]; p + 2 points at a[3], whose value is 8.

questions.questionText: In C++, which catch block ordering is correct when both a base-class exception and a derived-class exception are handled?
options: Order does not matter because the best match is chosen
catch (...) first, then the specific handlers
questions.explanation: Handlers are tried in order and a Base& handler also matches Derived objects, so the derived handler must come first; catch (...) must be last.
Adjacent string literals are joined during translation, so "NE" "C" is the single literal "NEC". It holds 3 characters plus one terminating '\0', so sizeof gives 4, and %s prints NEC.

6 & 3 is a bitwise AND (110 & 011 = 010), an int 2 that boolalpha does not affect, while 6 && 3 is a bool and prints as true. The parenthesised 1 << 3 is a shift giving 8; the following << 1 is stream insertion, so 1 is printed after it.
%o prints 45 in octal: 45 = 5 × 8 + 5, so 55. The loop adds the lowest bit and shifts right until n is 0, so it counts the 1-bits of 45 = 101101 in binary, which is 4.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing C (C11) with C++ (C++17) is NOT correct?
options: C++ allows two functions with the same name if their parameter lists differ; C does not
A C++ struct may contain member functions and access specifiers; a C struct may not
C++, like C, requires the keyword struct in every declaration of a structure variable, as in struct Point p;
C++ adds references such as int &r = x;, which must be bound to an object when declared; C has none
questions.explanation: In C++ the tag of a struct (or class) is itself a type name, so Point p; is enough, while C needs struct Point p; or a typedef. The other three statements are true.

options: Nothing is printed: the loop never ends
questions.explanation: An 8-bit unsigned char wraps modulo 256, so c takes 246, 248, 250, 252, 254 (5 values); then 254 + 2 = 256 wraps to 0 and c takes 0, 2, 4 (3 values) before it equals 6. The body runs 5 + 3 = 8 times; unsigned wrap-around is well defined.

options: Compile error: the call f(1) is ambiguous
questions.explanation: The using-directives make both functions visible, and since their parameter types differ they form one overload set. f(1) matches A::f(int) exactly, f(1.5) matches B::f(double), and for f('x') the promotion char → int beats the conversion to double.

options: Nothing is printed: the loop never ends
questions.explanation: s collects 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. When i becomes 4, continue in a do-while jumps to the condition test, not to the top of the body; 4 < 4 is false, so the loop ends with s = 6 and i = 4.

questions.questionText: Which printf call prints the value of sizeof(arr) with the conversion specifier that standard C (C99 and later) provides for size_t?
questions.explanation: sizeof yields a value of the unsigned type size_t, and C99 added the length modifier z for it, so %zu matches. %d expects an int, %p a pointer and %lf a double, so they do not match a size_t argument.

options: Compile error: 2 cannot initialise an A object
questions.explanation: arr[0] is built by A(1) and arr[1] from 2 through the converting constructor A(int), printing 1 and 2. arr[2] has no initialiser, so the default argument gives A(7), printing 7; then 2 + 7 = 9 is printed.

options: It compiles and prints two and half on separate lines
Compile error: the labels 1 << 1 and 5 / 2 both have the value 2
questions.explanation: Case labels must be integer constant expressions with distinct values. 'B' - 'A' is 1, 1 << 1 is 2, and 5 / 2 is also 2 because integer division truncates, so the repeated value 2 is a compile error.

pal compares the outermost characters and recurses inward until the pointers meet. For "level" every pair matches, so the result is 1; for "lever" the first pair (l, r) differs, && skips the recursive call and the result is 0.

f swaps the first and last of the n elements it is given and recurses on the part between them. f(a + 1, 4) swaps a[1] and a[4] (2 and 5), f(a + 2, 2) swaps a[2] and a[3] (3 and 4), and f(a + 3, 0) stops, so a becomes 1 5 4 3 2 6.

questions.questionText: What does the C standard say about the statement printf("%d\n", 2.5);?
options: It prints 2, because printf truncates the double to an int
The behaviour is undefined, because %d requires an int argument but a double is passed
It prints 3, because printf rounds the double to the nearest int
It is a compile error that every standard compiler must report
questions.explanation: printf cannot convert its variable arguments, so each specifier must match the promoted argument type. Passing a double for %d is undefined behaviour (compilers usually only warn); use %f, or write (int)2.5 to print 2.

Each row of w is a char[6] holding one string. w + 2 points to the whole row w[2], so *(w + 2) is that row and %s prints blue. p = w[1] points to the 'g' of "green", so *(p + 4) is w[1][4] = 'n'. w[0] + 1 points to the second character of "red", so %s prints ed.

questions.questionText: Which throw expression is caught by the handler catch (const std::exception &e)?
questions.explanation: A handler for const std::exception & matches std::exception and every class derived from it; std::out_of_range derives from std::logic_error, which derives from std::exception. An int, a std::string and a const char * are unrelated types, so they pass this handler by.
fs receives a copy of the structure, so s in main keeps 1 and 2. fu writes u->a through a pointer, and because all members of a union share the same storage, u.b reads that same int, 7.

options: Compile error: x is declared twice in main
questions.explanation: Inside the inner block, extern int x; refers to the file-scope x and hides the local x there, so x++ makes the global 6 and prints it. After the block the local x = 1 is visible again and is printed.

Member names are looked up in the static type: p is a Base*, and Base has no member extra, so line 3 fails even though p points to a Der. Virtual dispatch in line 1 only chooses which override runs, and line 4 converts the pointer to Der* first.
p + 1 points to t[1], and name[2] of "Sita" is 't'. (*(p + 2)).age is 41, and 41 % 10 = 1. p[2].name + 1 points one character into "Hari", so %s prints ari.

questions.questionText: Given int a[4][5];, which expression does NOT refer to the element a[2][3]?
questions.explanation: [] binds tighter than unary *, so *(a + 2)[3] means *((a + 2)[3]) = *a[5], the first element of a row that does not exist. The other three all reduce to *(*(a + 2) + 3), which is a[2][3].
vector<T> v(2) default-constructs its two elements (DD). Copying the vector copies every element with T's copy constructor (CC), and w then holds 2 elements.

The first call swaps the values with three XORs, giving x = 9 and y = 5. In xswap(&x, &x) both pointers name the same int, so *a ^= *b computes 9 ^ 9 = 0 and the value is lost; the later XORs leave 0.

A static local object is constructed the first time control reaches its declaration (base part first: B, then D) and is not rebuilt on the second call. It is destroyed after main returns, derived part first: d, then b.

questions.questionText: A C program opens an existing file with fopen(name, "r+"). Which open mode gives an fstream the same behaviour in C++?
questions.explanation: "r+" opens an existing file for reading and writing, keeps its contents and fails if the file is missing, exactly like ios::in | ios::out. Adding ios::trunc gives "w+", ios::out | ios::app gives "a" and ios::in | ios::app gives "a+".
operator<< receives a const B &, and print is virtual, so b.print(o) runs the version for the object's real class: B for b, D for r (a reference to d) and D for d.
The loops swap only the pointers, putting the words into strcmp order: apple, fig, pear. w[0] is "apple", and *w[2] is 'p', so 'p' + 1 prints as q.

A handler of pointer type also accepts a thrown pointer after a derived-to-base pointer conversion or a qualification conversion (adding const). So &d, a D *, is caught by catch (B *), and &n, an int *, by catch (const int *). The literal 0 is thrown as an int, and a handler never turns an int into a null pointer, so it reaches catch (...): B, P, O.

questions.questionText: Each of the following integer literals has the value 26. Which one is valid in C++14 and later but is NOT part of standard C11?
questions.explanation: Binary literals with the 0b prefix were added in C++14 (C gained them only in C23, although many compilers accept them as an extension). 0x1A (hexadecimal), 032 (octal) and 26UL (unsigned long) are all standard C11 constants.

A set keeps its strings in ascending order, compared character by character by code, and in ASCII 'A' (65) comes before 'a' (97), so the order is Apple, apple, fig, pear. begin() gives the smallest, Apple; lower_bound("b") gives the first element not less than "b", which is fig because apple < b < fig; rbegin() gives the largest, pear.

The result of ?: has the common type of its second and third operands, here double, whichever one is chosen. So sizeof gives 8, and the chosen operand 7 / 2 is computed as the int 3 and then converted to 3.0.
setw(5) with fill character '0' writes 00042, and hex writes 255 as ff, so the file holds 00042 ff. Reading back with >> gives the words 00042 and ff, and the first word has 5 characters.

In C the result of ?: is never an lvalue, so assigning to it is a compile error. In C++ it is an lvalue when both branches are lvalues of the same type, so the assignment goes to b and 3 0 is printed.

Private inheritance makes B's public members private in D, so D's own member sum may still use x and y (line 1). The using-declaration in D's public section makes x public again (line 2), but y stays private, so d.y in main fails.

questions.questionText: After cin >> n; fails because the user typed abc for the int n, which action lets the program discard that input and read n again?
options: Call cin.clear(); alone, because resetting the flags also removes abc from the buffer
Call cin.ignore(1000, '\n'); alone, because ignore also resets failbit
Nothing: the next cin >> n skips the bad characters automatically
questions.explanation: A failed extraction sets failbit, and every later read fails until cin.clear() resets it. clear does not remove the bad characters, so cin.ignore(1000, '\n') must then discard them; neither call alone is enough.
Parameters of type int *& are references to the caller's pointers, so sw really swaps p and q: p now points to y and q to x. *p += 10 makes y = 12, and *q reads x = 1.

questions.questionText: Given char name[20]; and int n;, why is the first call written scanf("%19s", name) without &, while the second is written scanf("%d", &n)?
options: An array name used as an argument is converted to a pointer to its first element, so name already supplies the address scanf needs
scanf stores a string in an internal buffer first, so it never needs the address of the array
C passes arrays by value, and scanf copies the whole array back to the caller when it returns
The & is optional for every scanf argument; it is only a matter of style
questions.explanation: scanf needs the address of every object it fills. For int n that is &n, while name used as an argument decays to &name[0], the address of the first char to store (&name has the same address but the type char (*)[20], not the char * that %s expects).

options: Compile error: *p++ cannot be assigned to
questions.explanation: Postfix ++ binds tighter than *, so *p++ += 1 adds 1 to the character p points at and then moves p on. Each letter becomes the next one (E→F, X→Y, A→B, M→N), and the loop stops at the '\0', 4 characters from the start.

options: Compile error: a vector<N> cannot be initialised from {1, 2, 3}
questions.explanation: {1, 2, 3} builds three N objects through the converting constructor N(int). In the first loop n is a copy of each element, so multiplying it by 10 leaves a unchanged; in the second loop n is a reference, so the elements really become 2, 3 and 4, and 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.

questions.questionText: A function is declared as void report(std::ostream &os);. Which objects can be passed to it as the argument?
options: std::cout and std::cerr, but not file or string streams
std::cout, std::cerr, a std::ofstream object and a std::ostringstream object
Only objects created as std::ostream itself, because a reference parameter does not accept derived classes
questions.explanation: cout and cerr are ostream objects, and ofstream and ostringstream are derived from ostream, so a base-class reference binds to all of them. This is why one report function or << overload works for the console, files and strings alike.
The queue releases 1, 4, 9, 16 in FIFO order and the stack receives them in that order, so 16 is on top and the size is 4. Two pops remove 16 and 9, leaving 4 on top.

boost is a friend, so it may change the private w, but its parameter is a non-const reference. The const object c cannot bind to Box &, so line 3 fails, whereas calling the const member function get() on c (line 2) is allowed.

questions.questionText: Consider these statements about C: (i) for int a[5];, the expressions a[3], *(a + 3) and 3[a] all name the same element; (ii) inside void f(int b[10]), sizeof(b) gives the size of the whole 10-element array; (iii) a static local variable is initialised only once and keeps its value between calls; (iv) fopen(name, "w") returns NULL when the file does not already exist. Which of them are true?
questions.explanation: (i) is true because a[i] is defined as *(a + i) and addition commutes. (ii) is false: an array parameter is really a pointer, so sizeof gives the pointer size; (iii) is true, and (iv) is false because "w" creates a missing file (it is "r" that fails).

a + b is evaluated first and materialises a temporary T(3); temp + a then constructs T(4) directly in c (C++17 guarantees no extra copy). The temporary dies at the end of the full expression (D3) before | is printed, and at the end of main c, b and a are destroyed in reverse order.

questions.questionText: v is a std::vector<int>. Which statement sorts v into descending (largest-first) order? Assume <algorithm> and <functional> are included and using namespace std; is in effect.
questions.explanation: sort puts the range in the order given by the comparison, so greater<int>() puts the largest value first. reverse only flips the current order, plain sort gives ascending order, and sorting the reversed view with greater<int>() also reads ascending from v.begin().

questions.questionText: Consider these statements about C++: (i) when an object of class D : public B, which has a member object M m, is created, the constructors run in the order B, M, D; (ii) a member function defined inside the class body is implicitly inline; (iii) a catch (...) handler may be placed before the other handlers of the same try block; (iv) in the diamond A → B, A → C, (B, C) → D with no virtual base classes, a D object contains only one A sub-object. Which of them are true?
questions.explanation: (i) is true: bases are built first, then members in declaration order, then the constructor body; (ii) is also true. (iii) is false because catch (...) must be the last handler, and (iv) is false because without virtual inheritance D holds two A sub-objects, one via B and one via C.
